references.authors: Harman D
references.title: Aging: a theory based on free radical and radiation chemistry
references.finding: Proposed that aging is caused by cumulative damage from free radicals formed during normal oxygen metabolism, and suggested that antioxidants might slow it.

references.authors: Harman D
references.title: The biologic clock: the mitochondria?
references.finding: Narrowed the free-radical theory to mitochondria, proposing them as both the main source and the main target of the radicals that set lifespan.

references.authors: Pérez VI, Bokov A, Van Remmen H, et al.
references.title: Is the oxidative stress theory of aging dead?
references.finding: Reviewed a large mouse programme: of 18 genetic manipulations of antioxidant enzymes, only Sod1 deletion changed lifespan (shortened it), and none extended it.

references.authors: Pérez VI, Van Remmen H, Bokov A, et al.
references.title: The overexpression of major antioxidant enzymes does not extend the lifespan of mice
references.finding: Mice overexpressing CuZnSOD, catalase, CuZnSOD plus catalase, or CuZnSOD plus MnSOD did not live longer than controls.

references.authors: Van Remmen H, Ikeno Y, Hamilton M, et al.
references.title: Life-long reduction in MnSOD activity results in increased DNA damage and higher incidence of cancer but does not accelerate aging
references.finding: Sod2+/- mice with 50% less MnSOD had more oxidative DNA damage (8-oxodG) and twice the tumour incidence, but identical mean and maximum lifespan.

references.authors: Zhang Y, Ikeno Y, Qi W, et al.
references.title: Mice deficient in both Mn superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase-1 have increased oxidative damage and a greater incidence of pathology but no reduction in longevity
references.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
references.finding: Mice lacking Gpx1 and half of Sod2 had more DNA and protein oxidation and more cancer, but no reduction in lifespan.

references.authors: Elchuri S, Oberley TD, Qi W, et al.
references.title: CuZnSOD deficiency leads to persistent and widespread oxidative damage and hepatocarcinogenesis later in life
references.finding: Sod1-knockout mice had widespread oxidative damage, more than 70% developed liver nodules or carcinoma, and they had shorter lives.

references.authors: Schriner SE, Linford NJ, Martin GM, et al.
references.title: Extension of murine life span by overexpression of catalase targeted to mitochondria
references.finding: Mice expressing catalase targeted to mitochondria (MCAT) lived about 5 months longer (median and maximum), with less oxidative damage, delayed cardiac pathology and cataracts.

references.authors: Treuting PM, Linford NJ, Knoblaugh SE, et al.
references.title: Reduction of age-associated pathology in old mice by overexpression of catalase in mitochondria
references.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
references.finding: MCAT mice had lower malignant (non-blood) tumour burden and fewer cardiac lesions at death, but no effect on blood cancers or kidney disease.

references.authors: Dai DF, Santana LF, Vermulst M, et al.
references.title: Overexpression of catalase targeted to mitochondria attenuates murine cardiac aging
references.finding: Mitochondrial catalase attenuated age-related cardiac hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, fibrosis and mitochondrial DNA mutations in mice.

references.authors: Andziak B, Buffenstein R
references.title: Disparate patterns of age-related changes in lipid peroxidation in long-lived naked mole-rats and shorter-lived mice
references.finding: Young naked mole-rats (lifespan >28 years) had at least twice the lipid peroxidation (urinary isoprostanes, liver MDA) of mice (lifespan ~3.5 years).

references.authors: Pérez VI, Buffenstein R, Masamsetti V, et al.
references.title: Protein stability and resistance to oxidative stress are determinants of longevity in the longest-living rodent, the naked mole-rat
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Naked mole-rats carry more lipid, protein and DNA oxidation than mice from a young age, but their proteins are more stable and their proteasome activity is higher.

references.authors: Lewis KN, Andziak B, Yang T, et al.
references.title: The naked mole-rat response to oxidative stress: just deal with it
references.finding: Naked mole-rats combine mouse-like ROS production and unexceptional antioxidant defences with high steady-state oxidative damage, yet stay healthy; they tolerate rather than prevent damage.

references.authors: Trifunovic A, Hansson A, Wredenberg A, et al.
references.title: Somatic mtDNA mutations cause aging phenotypes without affecting reactive oxygen species production
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: mtDNA mutator mice age prematurely from accumulated mtDNA mutations, but without any increase in ROS production, breaking the predicted 'vicious cycle'.

references.authors: Van Raamsdonk JM, Hekimi S
references.title: Deletion of the mitochondrial superoxide dismutase sod-2 extends lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans
references.finding: In C. elegans, deleting any of the five sod genes (singly or in combinations) did not shorten lifespan, and sod-2 deletion extended it despite more protein oxidation.

references.authors: Gems D, Doonan R
references.title: Antioxidant defense and aging in C. elegans: is the oxidative damage theory of aging wrong?
references.finding: Worm studies in which antioxidant defences were changed without changing lifespan challenge the oxidative damage theory of aging.

references.authors: Schulz TJ, Zarse K, Voigt A, et al.
references.title: Glucose restriction extends Caenorhabditis elegans life span by inducing mitochondrial respiration and increasing oxidative stress
references.finding: Glucose restriction extended worm lifespan by raising mitochondrial respiration and ROS; antioxidants abolished the extension, the first direct evidence for 'mitohormesis'.

references.authors: Ristow M, Zarse K, Oberbach A, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants prevent health-promoting effects of physical exercise in humans
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Vitamin C 1000 mg/day plus vitamin E 400 IU/day abolished the gain in insulin sensitivity and the induction of antioxidant genes from 4 weeks of exercise training.

references.authors: Ristow M, Zarse K
references.title: How increased oxidative stress promotes longevity and metabolic health: The concept of mitochondrial hormesis (mitohormesis)
references.finding: Defines mitohormesis: a transient rise in mitochondrial ROS during energy restriction or exercise triggers adaptive stress resistance, and antioxidants block the benefit.

references.authors: Ristow M
references.title: Unraveling the truth about antioxidants: mitohormesis explains ROS-induced health benefits
references.finding: Argues that mitohormesis explains why ROS produced during exercise and caloric restriction promote health and why antioxidant supplements fail or harm.

references.authors: Yun J, Finkel T
references.title: Mitohormesis
references.finding: Mild mitochondrial stress activates cytosolic signalling and nuclear gene expression that leave cells more resistant to later stress (mitohormesis).

references.authors: Sies H
references.title: Hydrogen peroxide as a central redox signaling molecule in physiological oxidative stress: Oxidative eustress
references.finding: Defines physiological H2O2 (about 1-10 nM) as 'oxidative eustress' that signals through specific cysteines; higher levels cause damage ('distress').

references.authors: Sies H, Belousov VV, Chandel NS, et al.
references.title: Defining roles of specific reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cell biology and physiology
references.finding: Expert recommendation: the generic term 'ROS' should not be used for specific molecules; H2O2 and superoxide have distinct signalling roles that need specific measurement.

references.authors: Gladyshev VN
references.title: The free radical theory of aging is dead. Long live the damage theory!
references.finding: Argues the free-radical theory is dead: ROS are one of many by-products of imperfect biological processes, and aging reflects accumulation of all such damage.

references.authors: Gladyshev VN
references.title: Aging: progressive decline in fitness due to the rising deleteriome adjusted by genetic, environmental, and stochastic processes
references.finding: Introduces the 'deleteriome': the sum of cumulative deleterious age-related changes at all levels, adjusted by genetic, environmental and stochastic processes, as a unifying model of aging.

references.authors: Barja G
references.title: Updating the mitochondrial free radical theory of aging: an integrated view, key aspects, and confounding concepts
references.finding: Defends an updated mitochondrial free-radical theory: long-lived animals have low mitochondrial ROS generation (complex I) and oxidation-resistant macromolecules; many criticisms rest on misconceptions.

references.authors: Kirkwood TB, Kowald A
references.title: The free-radical theory of ageing--older, wiser and still alive: modelling positional effects of the primary targets of ROS reveals new support
references.finding: Modelling of where ROS are generated relative to their targets suggests many negative experiments are misleading; the theory survives as one of several mechanisms of aging.

references.authors: Liochev SI
references.title: Reactive oxygen species and the free radical theory of aging
references.finding: Defends the traditional view that ROS cause direct damage contributing to aging, cautioning against an overcorrection that treats ROS mainly as beneficial signals.

references.authors: Speakman JR, Selman C
references.title: The free-radical damage theory: Accumulating evidence against a simple link of oxidative stress to ageing and lifespan
references.finding: Antioxidant-gene knockout mice show more oxidative damage but no change in lifespan, and long-lived species do not have exceptional defences: evidence against a simple damage-lifespan link.

references.authors: Lapointe J, Hekimi S
references.title: When a theory of aging ages badly
references.finding: Concludes the mitochondrial free-radical theory of aging should be considered refuted, citing long-lived Mclk1-/- mice and transgenic studies.

references.authors: Shields HJ, Traa A, Van Raamsdonk JM
references.title: Beneficial and Detrimental Effects of Reactive Oxygen Species on Lifespan: A Comprehensive Review of Comparative and Experimental Studies
references.finding: Comparative studies mostly show an inverse correlation between ROS damage and lifespan, but experimental manipulations show ROS can shorten, not affect, or extend lifespan depending on context.

references.authors: López-Otín C, Blasco MA, Partridge L, et al.
references.title: Hallmarks of aging: An expanding universe
references.finding: Updated framework of 12 hallmarks of aging, including mitochondrial dysfunction, genomic instability and chronic inflammation.

references.authors: Bjelakovic G, Nikolova D, Gluud LL, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant supplements for prevention of mortality in healthy participants and patients with various diseases
references.finding: Antioxidant supplements did not reduce mortality; in low-bias trials beta-carotene, vitamin E and higher-dose vitamin A slightly increased it (RR 1.04 overall).

references.authors: Singh P, Gollapalli K, Mangiola S, et al.
references.title: Taurine deficiency as a driver of aging
references.finding: Circulating taurine fell with age in mice, monkeys and humans; taurine supplementation extended mouse median lifespan and improved healthspan in mice and middle-aged monkeys; human low taurine correlated with age-related disease.

references.authors: McGaunn J, Baur JA
references.title: Taurine linked with healthy aging
references.finding: Science perspective on Singh et al.: reversing age-associated taurine loss improved mouse longevity and monkey health, but human trials are needed.

references.authors: Fernandez ME, Bernier M, Price NL, et al.
references.title: Is taurine an aging biomarker?
references.n: three human cohorts plus monkeys and mice
references.finding: Circulating taurine increased or stayed unchanged with age in three human cohorts, monkeys and mice measured longitudinally; links between taurine and health outcomes were inconsistent.

references.authors: Tzang CC, Chi LY, Lin LH, et al.
references.title: Taurine reduces the risk for metabolic syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Taurine 0.5-6 g/day lowered systolic BP by ~4 mmHg, diastolic BP by ~1.5 mmHg, fasting glucose by ~5.9 mg/dL and triglycerides by ~18 mg/dL, with no excess adverse effects.

references.authors: Sun Q, Wang B, Li Y, et al.
references.title: Taurine Supplementation Lowers Blood Pressure and Improves Vascular Function in Prehypertension: Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study
references.finding: Taurine 1.6 g/day for 12 weeks lowered clinic systolic BP by 7.2 vs 2.6 mmHg (placebo) and improved endothelial function.

references.authors: Waldron M, Patterson SD, Tallent J, et al.
references.title: The Effects of an Oral Taurine Dose and Supplementation Period on Endurance Exercise Performance in Humans: A Meta-Analysis
references.finding: Taurine 1-6 g taken acutely or for up to 2 weeks gave a small-to-moderate improvement in endurance performance (Hedges' g 0.40).

references.authors: Shao A, Hathcock JN
references.title: Risk assessment for the amino acids taurine, L-glutamine and L-arginine
references.finding: Risk assessment set an observed safe level for supplemental taurine of 3 g/day based on human trials, with no systematic adverse effects found.

references.authors: Kreider RB, Kalman DS, Antonio J, et al.
references.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine
references.finding: ISSN position stand: creatine monohydrate is the most effective ergogenic supplement for high-intensity exercise and lean mass, and is safe at recommended doses (3-5 g/day; up to 30 g/day for 5 years studied).

references.authors: Antonio J, Candow DG, Forbes SC, et al.
references.title: Common questions and misconceptions about creatine supplementation: what does the scientific evidence really show?
references.finding: Reviews misconceptions: creatine does not harm healthy kidneys, does not cause dehydration or cramps, and has no consistent link to hair loss.

references.authors: Devries MC, Phillips SM
references.title: Creatine supplementation during resistance training in older adults-a meta-analysis
references.finding: Adding creatine to resistance training in older adults increased fat-free mass and chest- and leg-press strength more than training alone.

references.authors: Chilibeck PD, Kaviani M, Candow DG, et al.
references.title: Effect of creatine supplementation during resistance training on lean tissue mass and muscular strength in older adults: a meta-analysis
references.finding: Creatine during resistance training added 1.37 kg lean mass and improved chest press (SMD 0.35) and leg press (SMD 0.24) strength.

references.authors: Avgerinos KI, Spyrou N, Bougioukas KI, et al.
references.title: Effects of creatine supplementation on cognitive function of healthy individuals: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Systematic review: creatine may improve short-term memory and reasoning in healthy people, especially vegetarians; other domains were inconsistent and young people showed little effect.

references.authors: Prokopidis K, Giannos P, Triantafyllidis KK, et al.
references.title: Effects of creatine supplementation on memory in healthy individuals: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Creatine improved memory overall (SMD 0.29), driven by older adults (SMD 0.88), with no effect in people aged 11-31.

references.authors: Eckert I, Pascher E
references.title: Letter to the Editor: Double-counting due to inadequate statistics leads to false-positive findings in "Effects of creatine supplementation on memory in healthy individuals: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials"
references.finding: Letter arguing the Prokopidis creatine-memory meta-analysis double-counted data, inflating a possibly false-positive result.

references.authors: Xu C, Bi S, Zhang W, et al.
references.title: The effects of creatine supplementation on cognitive function in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Creatine monohydrate improved memory (SMD 0.31) and attention time, with little effect on other cognitive domains.

references.authors: Gordji-Nejad A, Matusch A, Kleedörfer S, et al.
references.title: Single dose creatine improves cognitive performance and induces changes in cerebral high energy phosphates during sleep deprivation
references.finding: A single 0.35 g/kg creatine dose during 21 h of sleep deprivation changed brain high-energy phosphates and improved processing speed and cognitive performance.

references.authors: de Souza E Silva A, Pertille A, Reis Barbosa CG, et al.
references.title: Effects of Creatine Supplementation on Renal Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
references.finding: Creatine supplementation did not cause renal damage at studied doses and durations; small serum creatinine changes reflect creatine metabolism, not kidney injury.

references.authors: Writing Group for the NINDS Exploratory Trials in Parkinson Disease (NET-PD) Investigators; Kieburtz K, Tilley BC, Elm JJ, et al.
references.title: Effect of creatine monohydrate on clinical progression in patients with Parkinson disease: a randomized clinical trial
references.finding: Creatine 10 g/day for at least 5 years did not slow clinical progression of Parkinson disease; the trial was stopped for futility.

references.authors: Hersch SM, Schifitto G, Oakes D, et al.
references.title: The CREST-E study of creatine for Huntington disease: A randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Up to 40 g/day creatine for up to 48 months did not slow functional decline (stopped for futility); gastrointestinal side effects were more common.

references.authors: Sestili P, Martinelli C, Colombo E, et al.
references.title: Creatine as an antioxidant
references.finding: Reviews cell and animal evidence that creatine has direct and indirect antioxidant actions as part of its cytoprotective effects.

references.authors: Muccini AM, Tran NT, de Guingand DL, et al.
references.title: Creatine Metabolism in Female Reproduction, Pregnancy and Newborn Health
references.finding: Creatine metabolism supports energy in female reproductive tissues and placenta; antenatal creatine protects against birth asphyxia in animal models, but human evidence is lacking.

references.authors: LaRosa DA, Ellery SJ, Snow RJ, et al.
references.title: Maternal creatine supplementation during pregnancy prevents acute and long-term deficits in skeletal muscle after birth asphyxia: a study of structure and function of hind limb muscle in the spiny mouse
references.finding: In spiny mice, maternal creatine supplementation during pregnancy prevented asphyxia-induced skeletal muscle damage in offspring.

references.authors: Nedeljkovic D, Todorovic N, Javorac D, et al.
references.title: The effects of 8-week creatine supplementation with and without ubiquinol on sperm quality biomarkers in normospermic and oligospermic men: A randomized controlled pilot trial
references.finding: Exploratory pilot: 8 weeks of creatine (with or without ubiquinol) gave a non-significant trend toward higher sperm concentration.

references.authors: Sekhar RV, Patel SG, Guthikonda AP, et al.
references.title: Deficient synthesis of glutathione underlies oxidative stress in aging and can be corrected by dietary cysteine and glycine supplementation
references.finding: Older adults had about half the red-cell glutathione and synthesis rate of young adults; 2 weeks of cysteine (as NAC) plus glycine raised glutathione 94.6% and lowered F2-isoprostanes.

references.authors: Kumar P, Liu C, Hsu JW, et al.
references.title: Glycine and N-acetylcysteine (GlyNAC) supplementation in older adults improves glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, insulin resistance, endothelial dysfunction, genotoxicity, muscle strength, and cognition: Results of a pilot clinical trial
references.finding: Open-label pilot: 24 weeks of GlyNAC in 8 older adults corrected glutathione deficiency and improved many markers including strength, gait speed and cognition; benefits faded 12 weeks after stopping.

references.authors: Kumar P, Liu C, Suliburk J, et al.
references.title: Supplementing Glycine and N-Acetylcysteine (GlyNAC) in Older Adults Improves Glutathione Deficiency, Oxidative Stress, Mitochondrial Dysfunction, Inflammation, Physical Function, and Aging Hallmarks: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
references.finding: 16-week placebo-controlled RCT: GlyNAC improved glutathione, oxidative stress, mitochondrial fuel oxidation, inflammation, insulin resistance, gait speed and strength in older adults.

references.authors: Kumar P, Osahon OW, Sekhar RV
references.title: GlyNAC (Glycine and N-Acetylcysteine) Supplementation in Mice Increases Length of Life by Correcting Glutathione Deficiency, Oxidative Stress, Mitochondrial Dysfunction, Abnormalities in Mitophagy and Nutrient Sensing, and Genomic Damage
references.finding: GlyNAC-fed C57BL/6J mice lived 24% longer than controls in a single-lab study.

references.authors: Lizzo G, Migliavacca E, Lamers D, et al.
references.title: A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial in Healthy Older Adults to Determine Efficacy of Glycine and N-Acetylcysteine Supplementation on Glutathione Redox Status and Oxidative Damage
references.finding: Industry-run RCT: GlyNAC at 2.4, 4.8 or 7.2 g/day for 2 weeks did not raise glutathione or the GSH:GSSG ratio (primary endpoint); a post-hoc subgroup with high oxidative stress and low glutathione responded.

references.authors: Miller RA, Harrison DE, Astle CM, et al.
references.title: Glycine supplementation extends lifespan of male and female mice
references.finding: In the NIA Interventions Testing Program, an 8% glycine diet extended lifespan of male and female genetically heterogeneous mice by 4-6%.

references.authors: Bannai M, Kawai N, Ono K, et al.
references.title: The effects of glycine on subjective daytime performance in partially sleep-restricted healthy volunteers
references.finding: 3 g glycine before bed during 3 nights of 25% sleep restriction reduced daytime fatigue and improved psychomotor vigilance compared with placebo.

references.authors: Kawai N, Sakai N, Okuro M, et al.
references.title: The sleep-promoting and hypothermic effects of glycine are mediated by NMDA receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus
references.finding: In rats, glycine promoted NREM sleep and lowered core temperature via NMDA receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, causing peripheral vasodilation.

references.authors: Yoshino M, Yoshino J, Kayser BD, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide mononucleotide increases muscle insulin sensitivity in prediabetic women
references.finding: NMN 250 mg/day for 10 weeks increased muscle insulin sensitivity (clamp) and insulin signalling vs placebo.

references.authors: Brenner C
references.title: Comment on "Nicotinamide mononucleotide increases muscle insulin sensitivity in prediabetic women"
references.finding: Comment arguing the Yoshino NMN trial was not effectively randomized: the NMN group had far less liver fat at baseline (6.3% vs 14.8%).

references.authors: Elhassan YS, Kluckova K, Fletcher RS, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide Riboside Augments the Aged Human Skeletal Muscle NAD(+) Metabolome and Induces Transcriptomic and Anti-inflammatory Signatures
references.finding: NR 1 g/day for 21 days raised the muscle NAD+ metabolome and lowered inflammatory cytokines but did not change mitochondrial bioenergetics.

references.authors: Dollerup OL, Christensen B, Svart M, et al.
references.title: A randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial of nicotinamide riboside in obese men: safety, insulin-sensitivity, and lipid-mobilizing effects
references.finding: NR 2 g/day for 12 weeks was safe but did not improve insulin sensitivity, glucose metabolism, energy expenditure or body composition.

references.authors: Dollerup OL, Chubanava S, Agerholm M, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide riboside does not alter mitochondrial respiration, content or morphology in skeletal muscle from obese and insulin-resistant men
references.finding: NR 2 g/day for 12 weeks did not change muscle mitochondrial respiration, content or morphology, or muscle NAD+ levels.

references.authors: Martens CR, Denman BA, Mazzo MR, et al.
references.title: Chronic nicotinamide riboside supplementation is well-tolerated and elevates NAD(+) in healthy middle-aged and older adults
references.finding: NR 1 g/day for 6 weeks was well tolerated and raised blood NAD+ metabolism, with possible small benefits on blood pressure and arterial stiffness to be tested.

references.authors: Remie CME, Roumans KHM, Moonen MPB, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide riboside supplementation alters body composition and skeletal muscle acetylcarnitine concentrations in healthy obese humans
references.finding: NR 1 g/day for 6 weeks did not improve insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial function, liver fat or blood pressure; it slightly increased fat-free mass.

references.authors: Conze D, Brenner C, Kruger CL
references.title: Safety and Metabolism of Long-term Administration of NIAGEN (Nicotinamide Riboside Chloride) in a Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-controlled Clinical Trial of Healthy Overweight Adults
references.finding: NR 100, 300 or 1000 mg/day for 8 weeks raised whole-blood NAD+ by 22%, 51% and 142% with no excess adverse events.

references.authors: Trammell SA, Schmidt MS, Weidemann BJ, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide riboside is uniquely and orally bioavailable in mice and humans
references.finding: Single oral doses of 100-1000 mg NR produced dose-dependent rises in the blood NAD+ metabolome (industry-sponsored).

references.authors: Irie J, Inagaki E, Fujita M, et al.
references.title: Effect of oral administration of nicotinamide mononucleotide on clinical parameters and nicotinamide metabolite levels in healthy Japanese men
references.finding: Single-arm, non-randomized study: single oral NMN doses of 100-500 mg were safe and dose-dependently raised NAD+ breakdown products in plasma.

references.authors: Igarashi M, Nakagawa-Nagahama Y, Miura M, et al.
references.title: Chronic nicotinamide mononucleotide supplementation elevates blood nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide levels and alters muscle function in healthy older men
references.finding: NMN 250 mg/day for 6-12 weeks raised blood NAD+; gait speed and grip improvements were only nominally significant and body composition did not change.

references.authors: Yi L, Maier AB, Tao R, et al.
references.title: The efficacy and safety of β-nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) supplementation in healthy middle-aged adults: a randomized, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, dose-dependent clinical trial
references.finding: NMN 300-900 mg/day for 60 days raised blood NAD+ (plateau at 600 mg) and increased 6-minute walk distance; HOMA-IR did not change.

references.authors: Prokopidis K, Moriarty F, Bahat G, et al.
references.title: The Effect of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide and Riboside on Skeletal Muscle Mass and Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
references.finding: NMN did not improve skeletal muscle index, grip strength, gait speed or chair-stand time; evidence does not support NMN or NR for preserving muscle in older adults.

references.authors: Harrison DE, Strong R, Reifsnyder P, et al.
references.title: 17-a-estradiol late in life extends lifespan in aging UM-HET3 male mice; nicotinamide riboside and three other drugs do not affect lifespan in either sex
references.finding: In the NIA Interventions Testing Program, nicotinamide riboside did not extend lifespan in male or female mice.

references.authors: Freeberg KA, Udovich CC, Martens CR, et al.
references.title: Dietary Supplementation With NAD+-Boosting Compounds in Humans: Current Knowledge and Future Directions
references.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
references.finding: NAD+-boosting compounds are safe and raise NAD+ metabolites in human tissues, but small, heterogeneous trials limit conclusions about physiological benefit.

references.authors: Brakedal B, Dölle C, Riemer F, et al.
references.title: The NADPARK study: A randomized phase I trial of nicotinamide riboside supplementation in Parkinson's disease
references.n: 30 people with newly diagnosed Parkinson disease
references.finding: NR 1000 mg/day for 30 days raised brain NAD levels in some patients and lowered inflammatory cytokines, with mild clinical improvement in responders (phase I).

references.authors: Reiter RJ, Rosales-Corral S, Tan DX, et al.
references.title: Melatonin as a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant: one of evolution's best ideas
references.finding: Argues melatonin is a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant made within mitochondria, scavenging radicals and upregulating antioxidant enzymes (largely cell and animal data).

references.authors: Ghorbaninejad P, Sheikhhossein F, Djafari F, et al.
references.title: Effects of melatonin supplementation on oxidative stress: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Melatonin raised total antioxidant capacity and lowered MDA and protein carbonyls, with high heterogeneity and mostly patient populations.

references.authors: Ferracioli-Oda E, Qawasmi A, Bloch MH
references.title: Meta-analysis: melatonin for the treatment of primary sleep disorders
references.finding: Melatonin shortened sleep onset by about 7 minutes and lengthened total sleep by about 8 minutes in primary sleep disorders, with small improvement in sleep quality.

references.authors: Sateia MJ, Buysse DJ, Krystal AD, et al.
references.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Pharmacologic Treatment of Chronic Insomnia in Adults: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline
references.finding: AASM guideline: suggests clinicians not use melatonin for chronic insomnia in adults (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence).

references.authors: Zhdanova IV, Wurtman RJ, Regan MM, et al.
references.title: Melatonin treatment for age-related insomnia
references.finding: A physiological 0.3 mg melatonin dose restored sleep efficiency in older insomniacs; 3 mg caused hypothermia and melatonin levels persisting into daytime.

references.authors: Cruz-Sanabria F, Bruno S, Crippa A, et al.
references.title: Optimizing the Time and Dose of Melatonin as a Sleep-Promoting Drug: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis
references.finding: Melatonin's effect on sleep onset and total sleep rose with dose up to about 4 mg/day, and taking it about 3 hours before bedtime worked better.

references.authors: Erland LA, Saxena PK
references.title: Melatonin Natural Health Products and Supplements: Presence of Serotonin and Significant Variability of Melatonin Content
references.finding: Melatonin content ranged from -83% to +478% of label; over 71% of products were outside 10% of label and 26% contained serotonin.

references.authors: Cohen PA, Avula B, Wang YH, et al.
references.title: Quantity of Melatonin and CBD in Melatonin Gummies Sold in the US
references.finding: In US melatonin gummies, actual melatonin ranged from 74% to 347% of the label; only 3 of 25 were within 10%, and one contained undeclared CBD and no melatonin.

references.authors: Lelak K, Vohra V, Neuman MI, et al.
references.title: Pediatric Melatonin Ingestions - United States, 2012-2021
references.finding: US pediatric melatonin ingestions reported to poison centres rose 530% from 2012 to 2021, with more hospitalizations; five children needed ventilation and two died.

references.authors: Besag FMC, Vasey MJ, Lao KSJ, et al.
references.title: Adverse Events Associated with Melatonin for the Treatment of Primary or Secondary Sleep Disorders: A Systematic Review
references.finding: Systematic review: melatonin adverse events in sleep-disorder trials were generally mild and short-lived (e.g., daytime sleepiness, headache, dizziness), but long-term data are scarce.

references.authors: Besag FMC, Vasey MJ
references.title: Adverse events in long-term studies of exogenous melatonin
references.finding: Long-term (6 months or more) melatonin studies report few clinically significant adverse events, but placebo-controlled long-term data are scarce.

references.authors: Murphy MP, Hartley RC
references.title: Mitochondria as a therapeutic target for common pathologies
references.finding: Reviews mitochondria as drug targets in common diseases and mitochondria-targeted compounds such as MitoQ; few agents have reached clinical trials.

references.authors: Rossman MJ, Santos-Parker JR, Steward CAC, et al.
references.title: Chronic Supplementation With a Mitochondrial Antioxidant (MitoQ) Improves Vascular Function in Healthy Older Adults
references.finding: MitoQ 20 mg/day for 6 weeks improved brachial flow-mediated dilation by 42% in older adults with impaired endothelial function, and lowered aortic stiffness only in those with high baseline stiffness.

references.authors: Snow BJ, Rolfe FL, Lockhart MM, et al.
references.title: A double-blind, placebo-controlled study to assess the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoQ as a disease-modifying therapy in Parkinson's disease
references.finding: MitoQ 40 or 80 mg/day for 12 months did not slow Parkinson disease progression on any measure.

references.authors: Gane EJ, Weilert F, Orr DW, et al.
references.title: The mitochondria-targeted anti-oxidant mitoquinone decreases liver damage in a phase II study of hepatitis C patients
references.finding: MitoQ 40 or 80 mg/day for 28 days lowered liver enzymes (ALT) from baseline, but differences vs placebo were not significant and viral load was unchanged.

references.authors: Kirkman DL, Stock JM, Shenouda N, et al.
references.title: Effects of a mitochondrial-targeted ubiquinol on vascular function and exercise capacity in chronic kidney disease: a randomized controlled pilot study
references.finding: MitoQ 20 mg/day for 4 weeks improved flow-mediated dilation vs placebo but did not change exercise capacity (pilot).

references.authors: Linder BA, Stute NL, Hutchison ZJ, et al.
references.title: Acute high-dose MitoQ does not increase urinary kidney injury markers in healthy adults: a randomized crossover trial
references.finding: An acute high dose of MitoQ (100-160 mg) did not raise urinary kidney injury markers.

references.authors: Pham T, MacRae CL, Broome SC, et al.
references.title: MitoQ and CoQ10 supplementation mildly suppresses skeletal muscle mitochondrial hydrogen peroxide levels without impacting mitochondrial function in middle-aged men
references.finding: MitoQ 20 mg/day or CoQ10 200 mg/day for 6 weeks mildly lowered muscle mitochondrial H2O2 but did not change mitochondrial function, urinary F2-isoprostanes or plasma TBARS.

references.authors: Williamson J, Hughes CM, Cobley JN, et al.
references.title: The mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoQ, attenuates exercise-induced mitochondrial DNA damage
references.finding: 21 days of MitoQ 20 mg/day attenuated exercise-induced nuclear and mitochondrial DNA damage in lymphocytes and muscle; a single dose had no effect.

references.authors: Broome SC, Atiola RD, Braakhuis AJ, et al.
references.title: Mitochondria-targeted antioxidant supplementation does not affect muscle soreness or recovery of maximal voluntary isometric contraction force following muscle-damaging exercise in untrained men: a randomized clinical trial
references.finding: MitoQ 20 mg/day for 14 days did not reduce muscle soreness after eccentric exercise, delayed recovery of eccentric torque and increased creatine kinase.

references.authors: Petrov A, Perekhvatova N, Skulachev M, et al.
references.title: SkQ1 Ophthalmic Solution for Dry Eye Treatment: Results of a Phase 2 Safety and Efficacy Clinical Study in the Environment and During Challenge in the Controlled Adverse Environment Model
references.finding: SkQ1 eye drops improved some signs and symptoms of dry eye vs placebo over 29 days (phase 2).

references.authors: Brzheskiy VV, Efimova EL, Vorontsova TN, et al.
references.title: Results of a Multicenter, Randomized, Double-Masked, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Study of the Efficacy and Safety of Visomitin Eye Drops in Patients with Dry Eye Syndrome
references.finding: Visomitin (SkQ1) eye drops three times daily for 6 weeks improved tear film stability and dry eye symptoms vs placebo (company-funded).

references.authors: Anisimov VN, Egorov MV, Krasilshchikova MS, et al.
references.title: Effects of the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant SkQ1 on lifespan of rodents
references.finding: SkQ1 increased lifespan in some mouse strains and housing conditions, with effects strongly dependent on vivarium pathogen status and sex.

references.authors: Brendler T, Williamson EM
references.title: Astaxanthin: How much is too much? A safety review
references.finding: Of 87 human studies of natural astaxanthin, none found safety concerns, 35 at 12 mg/day or more; approved doses range 2-24 mg/day, and EFSA's 2 mg ADI was based on synthetic astaxanthin in rats.

references.authors: Ma B, Lu J, Kang T, et al.
references.title: Astaxanthin supplementation mildly reduced oxidative stress and inflammation biomarkers: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Astaxanthin modestly lowered blood MDA (SMD -0.95) and, in type 2 diabetes, IL-6; data on other markers were limited.

references.authors: Harrison DE, Strong R, Reifsnyder P, et al.
references.title: Astaxanthin and meclizine extend lifespan in UM-HET3 male mice; fisetin, SG1002 (hydrogen sulfide donor), dimethyl fumarate, mycophenolic acid, and 4-phenylbutyrate do not significantly affect lifespan in either sex at the doses and schedules used
references.finding: In the NIA Interventions Testing Program, astaxanthin extended median male mouse lifespan by 12%, with no significant effect in females or on 90th-percentile lifespan.

references.authors: Liu C, Dong X, Jia J, et al.
references.title: Effects of Astaxanthin Supplementation on Fatigue, Motor Function and Cognition: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
references.n: RCTs on fatigue, motor function and cognition
references.finding: Astaxanthin had no significant effect on reaction time and a marginal effect on cognitive accuracy, but improved exercise performance when combined with training.

references.authors: Ziegler D, Ametov A, Barinov A, et al.
references.title: Oral treatment with alpha-lipoic acid improves symptomatic diabetic polyneuropathy: the SYDNEY 2 trial
references.finding: Oral ALA 600, 1200 or 1800 mg/day for 5 weeks reduced neuropathy symptoms by about half vs 32% on placebo; higher doses caused more nausea and vomiting.

references.authors: Ziegler D, Low PA, Litchy WJ, et al.
references.title: Efficacy and safety of antioxidant treatment with α-lipoic acid over 4 years in diabetic polyneuropathy: the NATHAN 1 trial
references.finding: ALA 600 mg/day for 4 years did not improve the primary composite endpoint; some secondary impairment scores improved, and serious adverse events were more frequent (38% vs 28%).

references.authors: Mijnhout GS, Kollen BJ, Alkhalaf A, et al.
references.title: Alpha lipoic Acid for symptomatic peripheral neuropathy in patients with diabetes: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: IV ALA 600 mg/day for 3 weeks clinically reduced neuropathic symptoms; the clinical relevance of 3-5 weeks of oral ALA above 600 mg/day was unclear.

references.authors: Kucukgoncu S, Zhou E, Lucas KB, et al.
references.title: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) as a supplementation for weight loss: results from a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: ALA produced a small short-term weight loss of 1.27 kg more than placebo.

references.authors: Gullo D, Evans JL, Sortino G, et al.
references.title: Insulin autoimmune syndrome (Hirata Disease) in European Caucasians taking α-lipoic acid
references.finding: Six European patients developed insulin autoimmune syndrome with severe hypoglycaemia 30-120 days after starting ALA 600 mg/day, linked to HLA-DRB1*04:03.

references.authors: Harris CB, Chowanadisai W, Mishchuk DO, et al.
references.title: Dietary pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) alters indicators of inflammation and mitochondrial-related metabolism in human subjects
references.finding: PQQ 0.2-0.3 mg/kg briefly lowered CRP and IL-6 and altered urinary metabolites in a tiny short study.

references.authors: Hwang PS, Machek SB, Cardaci TD, et al.
references.title: Effects of Pyrroloquinoline Quinone (PQQ) Supplementation on Aerobic Exercise Performance and Indices of Mitochondrial Biogenesis in Untrained Men
references.finding: PQQ 20 mg/day during 6 weeks of endurance training raised muscle PGC-1alpha protein but did not improve aerobic performance vs placebo.

references.authors: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA)
references.title: Safety of pyrroloquinoline quinone disodium salt as a novel food pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 258/97
references.finding: EFSA judged PQQ disodium salt safe as a novel food in supplements up to 20 mg/day for healthy adults (not pregnant or lactating women).

references.authors: Itoh Y, Hine K, Miura H, et al.
references.title: Effect of the Antioxidant Supplement Pyrroloquinoline Quinone Disodium Salt (BioPQQ™) on Cognitive Functions
references.finding: PQQ 20 mg/day for 12 weeks reduced decline on a Stroop interference test; other effects appeared only in subgroups.

references.authors: Shiojima Y, Takahashi M, Takahashi R, et al.
references.title: Effect of Dietary Pyrroloquinoline Quinone Disodium Salt on Cognitive Function in Healthy Volunteers: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Parallel-Group Study
references.finding: PQQ disodium salt 21.5 mg/day for 12 weeks improved several computerized cognitive scores vs placebo (manufacturer-linked trial).

references.authors: Ames BN
references.title: Prolonging healthy aging: Longevity vitamins and proteins
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Proposed 'longevity vitamins', including ergothioneine, PQQ and astaxanthin, and taurine as a conditional vitamin, based largely on mechanistic and observational reasoning.

references.authors: Boldyrev AA, Aldini G, Derave W
references.title: Physiology and pathophysiology of carnosine
references.finding: Carnosine (beta-alanyl-L-histidine) is abundant in muscle and brain and acts as a pH buffer, metal chelator, antioxidant and anti-glycation agent in experimental models.

references.authors: de Courten B, Jakubova M, de Courten MP, et al.
references.title: Effects of carnosine supplementation on glucose metabolism: Pilot clinical trial
references.finding: Carnosine 2 g/day for 12 weeks prevented a rise in fasting insulin and insulin resistance seen on placebo (pilot).

references.authors: Menon K, Marquina C, Liew D, et al.
references.title: Histidine-containing dipeptides reduce central obesity and improve glycaemic outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Histidine-containing dipeptides (carnosine, anserine) lowered waist circumference by 3.5 cm and HbA1c by 0.76%, with smaller effects in low-bias trials.

references.authors: Matthews JJ, Dolan E, Swinton PA, et al.
references.title: Effect of Carnosine or β-Alanine Supplementation on Markers of Glycemic Control and Insulin Resistance in Humans and Animals: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
references.finding: Carnosine or beta-alanine may lower fasting glucose, HbA1c and HOMA-IR in humans, based on only four human studies.

references.authors: Masuoka N, Lei C, Li H, et al.
references.title: Anserine, HClO-scavenger, protected against cognitive decline in individuals with mild cognitive impairment
references.finding: Anserine 500 mg/day for 12 weeks improved MMSE change score vs placebo (1.9 vs 0 points).

references.authors: Gründemann D, Harlfinger S, Golz S, et al.
references.title: Discovery of the ergothioneine transporter
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Identified OCTN1 (SLC22A4) as a dedicated ergothioneine transporter; cells expressing it accumulate and retain dietary ergothioneine.

references.authors: Halliwell B, Cheah IK, Tang RMY
references.title: Ergothioneine - a diet-derived antioxidant with therapeutic potential
references.finding: Ergothioneine is a diet-derived thiol antioxidant concentrated by a specific transporter, with protective effects in cell and animal models and therapeutic potential still untested in humans.

references.authors: Smith E, Ottosson F, Hellstrand S, et al.
references.title: Ergothioneine is associated with reduced mortality and decreased risk of cardiovascular disease
references.finding: Higher plasma ergothioneine was associated with lower coronary disease (HR 0.85/SD), cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.79) and overall mortality (HR 0.86) over 21 years.

references.authors: Cheah IK, Tang RM, Yew TS, et al.
references.title: Administration of Pure Ergothioneine to Healthy Human Subjects: Uptake, Metabolism, and Effects on Biomarkers of Oxidative Damage and Inflammation
references.finding: Oral pure ergothioneine was avidly absorbed and retained; oxidative damage and inflammation markers showed mostly non-significant downward trends.

references.authors: Cheah IK, Feng L, Tang RMY, et al.
references.title: Ergothioneine levels in an elderly population decrease with age and incidence of cognitive decline; a risk factor for neurodegeneration?
references.finding: Whole-blood ergothioneine declined after age 60 and was lower in people with mild cognitive impairment.

references.authors: Yau YF, Cheah IK, Mahendran R, et al.
references.title: Investigating the efficacy of ergothioneine to delay cognitive decline in mild cognitively impaired subjects: A pilot study
references.finding: Ergothioneine 25 mg three times weekly for one year was safe, improved a verbal learning test and stabilized neurofilament light chain vs placebo (pilot).

references.authors: Ba DM, Gao X, Al-Shaar L, et al.
references.title: Prospective study of dietary mushroom intake and risk of mortality: results from continuous National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2003-2014 and a meta-analysis
references.finding: Mushroom intake was associated with slightly lower all-cause mortality (pooled RR 0.94) in cohort studies; the NHANES analysis alone was non-significant.

references.authors: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA)
references.title: Statement on the safety of synthetic l-ergothioneine as a novel food - supplementary dietary exposure and safety assessment for infants and young children, pregnant and breastfeeding women
references.finding: EFSA concluded synthetic L-ergothioneine is safe as a novel food at proposed use levels, including for pregnant and breastfeeding women and young children (NOAEL 800 mg/kg/day).

references.authors: Ramsay RR, Dunford C, Gillman PK
references.title: Methylene blue and serotonin toxicity: inhibition of monoamine oxidase A (MAO A) confirms a theoretical prediction
references.finding: Methylene blue is a potent, tight-binding inhibitor of MAO-A, explaining serotonin toxicity when given to patients on SSRIs.

references.authors: Gillman PK
references.title: CNS toxicity involving methylene blue: the exemplar for understanding and predicting drug interactions that precipitate serotonin toxicity
references.finding: 13 of 14 reported cases of CNS toxicity with methylene blue met criteria for serotonin toxicity; even 0.75-1 mg/kg reaches MAO-A-inhibiting levels, so serotonergic drugs are a major hazard.

references.authors: Rojas JC, Bruchey AK, Gonzalez-Lima F
references.title: Neurometabolic mechanisms for memory enhancement and neuroprotection of methylene blue
references.finding: Reviews animal evidence that low-dose methylene blue cycles electrons in the respiratory chain, enhances cytochrome oxidase and memory, and is neuroprotective.

references.authors: Rodriguez P, Zhou W, Barrett DW, et al.
references.title: Multimodal Randomized Functional MR Imaging of the Effects of Methylene Blue in the Human Brain
references.finding: A single low oral dose of methylene blue increased fMRI responses during attention and memory tasks and raised correct memory retrieval by 7%.

references.authors: Gauthier S, Feldman HH, Schneider LS, et al.
references.title: Efficacy and safety of tau-aggregation inhibitor therapy in patients with mild or moderate Alzheimer's disease: a randomised, controlled, double-blind, parallel-arm, phase 3 trial
references.finding: LMTM (a stabilized reduced methylene blue) at 75 or 125 mg twice daily for 15 months did not slow cognitive or functional decline (negative primary analysis).

references.authors: van Maanen E, Gonçalves A, Chen L, et al.
references.title: Atypical population pharmacokinetics of hydromethylthionine in patients with Alzheimer's disease explains unexpected phase 3 trial results
references.finding: TauRx-affiliated pharmacokinetic modelling argued that the 4 mg methylthioninium 'control' in LMTM phase 3 trials reached active plasma levels, explaining unexpected symptomatic effects in the control arm.

references.authors: Alda M, McKinnon M, Blagdon R, et al.
references.title: Methylene blue treatment for residual symptoms of bipolar disorder: randomised crossover study
references.finding: Methylene blue 195 mg/day vs 15 mg added to lamotrigine improved residual depression and anxiety, but not cognition.

references.authors: Harrison DE, Strong R, Allison DB, et al.
references.title: Acarbose, 17-α-estradiol, and nordihydroguaiaretic acid extend mouse lifespan preferentially in males
references.finding: In the NIA Interventions Testing Program, methylene blue did not change median lifespan of male or female mice (small rise in female maximum lifespan).

references.authors: Harrison DE, Strong R, Sharp ZD, et al.
references.title: Rapamycin fed late in life extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice
references.finding: Rapamycin fed from 600 days of age extended median and maximal lifespan of male and female genetically heterogeneous mice (90th-percentile age +14% females, +9% males).

references.authors: Mannick JB, Del Giudice G, Lattanzi M, et al.
references.title: mTOR inhibition improves immune function in the elderly
references.finding: The rapalog everolimus (RAD001) for 6 weeks improved influenza vaccine response by about 20% and lowered PD-1-positive T cells.

references.authors: Mannick JB, Morris M, Hockey HP, et al.
references.title: TORC1 inhibition enhances immune function and reduces infections in the elderly
references.finding: Low-dose TORC1 inhibition for 6 weeks was associated with fewer reported infections over a year and better influenza vaccine response.

references.authors: Lamming DW, Ye L, Katajisto P, et al.
references.title: Rapamycin-induced insulin resistance is mediated by mTORC2 loss and uncoupled from longevity
references.finding: In mice, chronic rapamycin causes insulin resistance by disrupting mTORC2, while lifespan extension is linked to mTORC1 inhibition.

references.authors: Moel M, Harinath G, Lee V, et al.
references.title: Influence of rapamycin on safety and healthspan metrics after one year: PEARL trial results
references.finding: Compounded rapamycin 5 or 10 mg weekly for 48 weeks was relatively safe but did not change visceral fat (primary outcome); lean mass and pain improved only in women on 10 mg.

references.authors: Kaeberlein TL, Green AS, Haddad G, et al.
references.title: Evaluation of off-label rapamycin use to promote healthspan in 333 adults
references.finding: Survey of off-label rapamycin users was presented as initial evidence that rapamycin can be used safely in healthy adults; data are self-reported and uncontrolled, and several authors have commercial ties to longevity medicine.

references.authors: Lee DJW, Hodzic Kuerec A, Maier AB
references.title: Targeting ageing with rapamycin and its derivatives in humans: a systematic review
references.finding: Systematic review: rapamycin and rapalogs improved some immune, cardiovascular and skin ageing measures; in patients with disease they increased infections and blood lipids.

references.authors: US Food and Drug Administration, Human Foods Program
references.title: Response letter to Natural Products Association and Alliance for Natural Health USA regarding the regulatory status of beta-nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), Docket FDA-2023-P-0872
references.finding: FDA reversed its 2022 position and determined that NMN is not excluded from the dietary supplement definition, granting the industry petition in part (September 29, 2025).

references.authors: US Food and Drug Administration
references.title: Submitted 75-Day Premarket Notifications for New Dietary Ingredients
references.finding: Lists new-dietary-ingredient notifications for beta-NMN (NDIN 1444, filed November 2025, FDA response January 2026) and reduced NMN (NDIN 1451).
